question: For user-impacting generated media, what transparency controls and output-testing checks should be addressed under the technical standard?
draft:
**Direct answer.** Under the Australian Government AI Technical Standard, user-impacting generated media triggers mandatory watermarking and disclosure controls (Statement 8, Criteria 22–24) [1], reinforced by the human-centred transparency mechanism in Statement 10 (Criterion 33) [5]. Output-testing checks are addressed separately under Statement 27 (Criteria 95–100) [6], with the Evaluate section listing the required test criteria [7].

**Transparency controls for generated media (Statement 8 — Agencies must)**

- Apply visual watermarks and metadata to generated media content to provide transparency and provenance, including authorship [1]. This applies only where AI-generated content may directly impact a user; the standard's example is that using AI to generate a team logo would not need to be watermarked [1].
- Apply watermarks and metadata that are WCAG compatible where relevant [1].
- Apply visual and accessible content to indicate when a user is interacting with an AI system [3].

**Recommended (Agencies should) under Statement 8**

- For hidden watermarks, use watermarking tools based on the use case and content risk [3].
- Assess watermarking risks and limitations [3].

**Related transparency mechanism (Statement 10 — Agencies must)**

Criterion 33 requires establishing a mechanism to inform users of AI interactions and output, as part of transparency [5]. Depending on use case this may include incorporating visual cues on the AI product when applicable, informing users when text, audio or visual messages addressed to them are generated by AI, and including visual watermarks to identify content generated by AI [5].

**Output-testing checks (Statement 27 — Agencies must)**

- Undertake human verification of test design and implementation for correctness, consistency, and completeness [6].
- Conduct functional performance testing to verify the correctness of the SUT as per the pre-defined metrics [6].
- Perform controllability testing to verify human oversight and control, and system control requirements [6].
- Perform explainability and transparency testing as per the requirements, including testing that AI outputs are understandable for the target audience (with diversity of test subjects and representativeness of the target population) and that the right information is available for the right user [6].
- Perform calibration testing as per the requirements [6].
- Perform logging tests as per the requirements, verifying the system records system warnings and errors and relevant system changes with details of who made the change, timestamp, and system version [6].

The Evaluate section lists these as required criteria under Statement 27, alongside Statement 26 (mitigate bias in the testing process; define test criteria approaches) and Statement 28 (test for safety, robustness, and reliability) [7].

**Evidence gaps.** The available excerpts do not establish any testing criterion specifically scoped to verifying that watermarks or provenance metadata are correctly applied to generated media, nor any requirement to test watermark robustness or removal resistance. Statement 8's risk assessment content (Criterion 26) is referenced in the parent context but is not supported by the retained child excerpts [1][3].

child_citations.title: Australian Government AI Technical Standard
child_citations.quote:
Statement 4: Enable AI auditing Agencies must: Criterion 9: Provide end-to-end auditability. End-to-end AI auditability refers to the ability to trace and inspect the decisions and processes involved in the AI system lifecycle. This enables internal and external scrutiny. Publishing audit results enables public accountability, transparency, and trust. This may include: o establishing documentation across the AI system lifecycle as agreed with the accountable official. This should demonstrate conformance with the AI technical standard, and compliance with relevant legislation and regulations.

o establishing traceability of decisions and changes from requirements through to operational impacts o ensuring accessibility, availability, and explainability of technical and non-technical information to assist audits o ensuring audit logging of the AI tools and systems are configured appropriately This may include: ◦ enabling or disabling the capture of system inputs and outputs ◦ detect and record modifications to the system’s operation or performance ◦ record who made the modification, under what authority, and the rationale for the modification ◦ record system version and any other critical system information. o reviewing of audit logs o ensuring independence and avoiding conflict of interest when undertaking AI audits. Criterion 10: Perform ongoing data-specific checks across the AI lifecycle. This should address: o data quality for AI training, capabilities, and limitations o how data was evaluated for bias o controls to detect and manage data poisoning o legislative compliance. Criterion 11: Perform ongoing model-specific checks across the AI lifecycle.

child_citations.title: Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI
child_citations.quote:
• Testing entire agent workflows: Agents can take multiple steps in sequence without human involvement. Thus, beyond testing an agent’s final output, agents should be tested across their entire workflow, including reasoning and tool calling.

• Testing agents individually and together: Beyond individual agents, testing should be carried out at the multi -agent system level, to understand any emergent risks and behaviours when agents collaborate, such as competitive behaviours or the impact on other agents when one agent has been compromised.

• Testing in real or realistic environments: As agents may be expected to navigate real -world situations, testing should occur in a properly configured execution environment that mirrors production as closely as possible, such as using tool integrations, external APIs, and sandboxes that behave as th ey would in deployment. However, organisations should calibrate the need for realism against the risk of prematurely allowing agents to access tools that affect the real world.

• Testing repeatedly and across varied datasets: Agent behaviour is inherently stochastic and context dependent. Testing should thus be done at scale and across varied datasets to observe any unexpected low -probability behaviours, especially if they are of high-impact. This requires generating test datasets that cover different conditions that agents may encounter . These tests should also be run multiple times to check for stability ( e.g. the same inputs and contexts render consistent outputs), including minor perturbations where needed.

child_citations.title: Australian Government AI Technical Standard
child_citations.quote:
Statement 10: Adopt a human-centred approach Agencies must: Criterion 32: Identify human values requirements. Human values represent what people deem important in life such as autonomy, simplicity, tradition, achievement, and social recognition. Refer to human value requirements for AI systems paper. This includes: o using traditional requirement elicitation techniques such as surveys, interviews, group discussions and workshops to capture relevant human values for the AI use case o translating human values into technical requirements, which may vary depending on the risk level and AI use case o reviewing feedback to identify ignored human-values in the AI system o understanding the hierarchy of human values and emphasising those with higher relevance o considering social, economic, political, ethical, and legal values when designing AI systems o considering human values that are domain specific and based on the context of the AI system. Criterion 33: Establish a mechanism to inform users of AI interactions and output, as part of transparency.

Depending on use case this may include: o incorporating visual cues on the AI product when applicable o informing users when text, audio or visual messages addressed to them are generated by AI o including visual watermarks to identify content generated by AI o providing transparency on whether a user is interacting with a person, or system o including a disclaimer on the limitations of the system o displaying the relevance and currency of the information being provided o persona level transparency adhering to need-to-know principles

child_citations.title: Australian Government AI Technical Standard
child_citations.quote:
Statement 27: Test for specified behaviour Agencies must:

Criterion 95: Undertake human verification of test design and implementation for correctness, consistency, and completeness.

Criterion 96: Conduct functional performance testing to verify the correctness of the SUT as per the pre-defined metrics. This includes testing for fairness and bias to inform affirmative actions. For off-the-shelf systems, consider benchmark testing using industry-standard benchmark suites and comparisons with competing AI systems. Criterion 97: Perform controllability testing to verify human oversight and control, and system control requirements.

Criterion 98: Perform explainability and transparency testing as per the requirements. This involves: o testing that AI outputs are understandable for the target audience, ensuring diversity of test subjects and representativeness of the target population o testing that the right information is available for the right user. Criterion 99: Perform calibration testing as per the requirements. This involves: o measuring functional performance across various operating or installation conditions o testing that changes in calibration parameters are detected o testing that any out-of-range calibration parameters are rejected by the AI system in a transparent and explainable way. Criterion 100: Perform logging tests as per the requirements. This involves verifying that the system records: o system warnings and errors o relevant system changes with corresponding details of who made the change, timestamp, and system version.

Statement 27: Test for specified behaviour Required • Criterion 95: Undertake human verification of test design and implementation for correctness, consistency, and completeness. • Criterion 96: Conduct functional performance testing to verify the correctness of the AI system Under Test (SUT) as per the pre-defined metrics. • Criterion 97: Perform controllability testing to verify human oversight and control, and system control requirements. • Criterion 98: Perform explainability and transparency testing as per the requirements.

Statement 28: Test for safety, robustness, and reliability Required • Criterion 101: Test the computational performance of the system. • Criterion 102: Test safety measures through negative testing methods, failure testing, and fault injection. • Criterion 103: Test reliability of the AI output, through stress testing over an extended period, simulating edge cases, and operating under extreme conditions. Recommended • Criterion 104: Undertake adversarial testing (red team testing), attempting to break security and privacy measures to identify weaknesses.

child_citations.section_title: Statement 22: Implement model creation, tuning, and grounding
child_citations.title: Australian Government AI Technical Standard
child_citations.quote:
Statement 22: Implement model creation, tuning, and grounding Agencies must: Criterion 79: Set assessment criteria for the AI model, with respect to pre-defined metrics for the AI system. These criteria should address: o success factors specific to user stories o model quality thresholds and performance of the AI system o explainability and interpretability requirements o security and privacy requirements o ethics requirements o tolerance for error for model outputs o tolerance for negative impacts o error rates by scale and similar processing by humans. Considerations for modelling include: o model training, maintenance, and support costs o data and compute infrastructure constraints o likelihood of the AI models becoming outdated o whether the model can be legally used for the intended use case

o whether methods can be implemented to mitigate risk of new harms being introduced into the AI system o bias, security, and ethical concerns o whether the model meets the explainability and interpretability requirements o use of model interpretability tools to analyse important features and decision logic. Criterion 80: Identify and address situations when AI outputs should not be provided. These situations include: o low confidence scores o when user input and context are ambiguous or lack reliable sources o complex questions as input o limited knowledge base o privacy concerns and potential breach of safety o harmful content o unlawful content o misleading content. For GenAI, implementing techniques such as threshold settings or content filtering could address these situations.
